title: Meeting a friend at a juice bar in Rio
setting: It's a hot afternoon in Ipanema, Rio de Janeiro. You meet your friend Lucas at a busy juice bar on the corner, with dozens of fresh fruits hanging above the counter.
objectives: Greet a friend the Brazilian way
Understand everyday words like "a gente" and "beleza"
Accept a plan and say thanks casually
varietyNote: This is Brazilian Portuguese as heard in Rio de Janeiro. It differs from European Portuguese in pronunciation and many everyday words — juice is "suco" in Brazil but "sumo" in Portugal (see the Lisbon adventure). Brazil itself has many regional accents; in parts of the south and northeast, for example, people use "tu" as well as "você".

phrases.text: Me vê um suco de laranja, por favor.
phrases.translation: Can I get an orange juice, please?
phrases.example: Me vê um suco de manga e um pão de queijo, por favor.
phrases.exampleTranslation: Can I get a mango juice and a cheese bread, please?
phrases.note: "Me vê…" (literally "see me…") is a very common, friendly way to order in Brazil.

alsoHeard.text: Eu queria um suco de laranja, por favor.

phrases.example: Um suco de abacaxi sem açúcar, por favor.
phrases.exampleTranslation: A pineapple juice with no sugar, please.
phrases.note: Juice bars often add sugar unless you ask them not to.

phrases.example: A gente pode ir à praia depois.
phrases.exampleTranslation: We can go to the beach later.
phrases.note: In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, "a gente" is used far more than "nós" for "we". The verb goes in the "ele/ela" form.
A casual "thanks" among friends and in relaxed places. "Obrigado/obrigada" is the standard word.

cultureNotes: Juice bars ("casas de suco") are everywhere in Rio, with fresh juices from dozens of fruits — and often açaí served in a bowl ("açaí na tigela").
Brazilians commonly greet friends with a kiss on the cheek — how many varies by region and person — or a hug.
"Você" is the normal word for "you" in Rio. "O senhor / a senhora" is for showing respect to older people.
Plans are often relaxed: "depois" (later) and "já já" (in a bit) can be flexible!

steps.text: Lucas waves at you from the counter and greets you with a hug.

steps.prompt: How do you answer your friend?

options.why: The natural reply: "All good, and you?"

options.text: Estou bem, obrigado. E o senhor?
options.why: "O senhor" is formal ("sir") — far too formal for a friend.
"Yes" on its own sounds odd. Reply with "Tudo bem" and ask him back.

steps.prompt: You'd like an orange juice. How do you order, Rio-style?

options.text: Me vê um suco de laranja, por favor.
Dá-me um sumo de laranja, por favor.
options.why: That's European Portuguese — "sumo" is juice in Portugal. In Brazil it's "suco".

options.text: Eu quero comprar um laranja suco.
options.why: The word order is off — it's "um suco de laranja" (a juice of orange). And "Eu quero comprar…" (I want to buy…) sounds stiff when ordering.

options.text: Whether you want sugar in your juice
options.why: Right — juice bars often add sugar unless you say "sem açúcar".

options.text: Whether you want it with or without the peel
options.why: It's about sugar. The peel would be "casca".

steps.speaker: Lucas
steps.text: Bora pra praia depois? A gente pode ver o pôr do sol no Arpoador.
steps.translation: Shall we go to the beach later? We can watch the sunset at Arpoador.

steps.prompt: What does "a gente" mean in what Lucas said?

options.why: In everyday Brazilian Portuguese, "a gente" means "we" — much more common than "nós" in conversation.

options.text: The people (other people at the beach)
options.why: Literally "the people", but in conversation it means "we".

steps.prompt: You love the idea. How do you say yes, casually?

options.why: "Cool, sounds good!" — relaxed and very Brazilian.
"Yes, I accept your invitation" — correct, but much too formal between friends.
That's Spanish (from Spain). In Brazil, say "Beleza!" or "Pode ser!".

steps.text: Lucas insists on paying for your juice.

steps.prompt: How do you thank him, casually?

options.why: "I'm very grateful for your kindness" — lovely, but far too formal for a juice between friends.
"De nada" means "you're welcome" — the reply to thanks, not the thanks itself.
